lead: An RF amplifier is linear only for small signals. Push the input harder and the output compresses; apply two close tones and the amplifier creates new tones that were not at the input. Those effects set the strongest signal a receiver can handle and the weakest that survives beside it. Gain compression, intermodulation, intercept points and dynamic range turn “linear enough” into numbers on a datasheet and a specification for a phone, a base station or a radar front end.
prereq: You need: 5.2 for noise floor and sensitivity, and dB and dBm from Unit 2.

sections.h3: Gain compression and the 1 dB point

blocks.text: An amplifier's transfer curve is not a straight line. A simple model is y = a1x + a2x² + a3x³ + …, where x is the input voltage, y is the output voltage, and a1, a2 and a3 are constants. The a1 term is the wanted linear gain. Feed a sine wave of amplitude A volts and the small-signal gain becomes a1 + (3/4)a3A². Gain falls as A rises only when a3 < 0; that is the compression case used here. A positive a3 gives gain expansion at low drive. The a2 term makes second-order products and a DC shift. Amplitude-to-amplitude (AM-AM) conversion is this change of output amplitude with input amplitude, with no change of frequency.

At low power the output rises 1 dB for every 1 dB of input; on a dB plot the slope is 1. At high power the measured curve bends below that straight line. The 1 dB compression point is the input power where the measured output is 1 dB below the straight-line output. Call that input P1dB,in, in dBm. Call the measured output at that same input P1dB,out, also in dBm; this is the number datasheets quote. Because the measured output is 1 dB below the straight line, P1dB,out = P1dB,in + G − 1 dB, which gives P1dB,in = P1dB,out + 1 dB − G, where G is the small-signal gain in dB. The straight-line output at P1dB,in is P1dB,in + G, which is P1dB,out + 1 dB. Some syllabi call the compressed output P1dBc; here the 1 dB drop is stated separately to avoid confusion.

blocks.where: P1dB,in is the input 1 dB compression point in dBm; P1dB,out is the measured output at that input in dBm, already 1 dB below the straight line; G is the small-signal gain in dB. The straight-line output at P1dB,in is P1dB,out + 1 dB.

blocks.text: Back-off is how far a signal sits below P1dB,in. A large off-channel blocker can push an amplifier into compression and reduce gain for a weak wanted signal; that is blocking. The figure uses G = 20 dB and a measured P1dB,out = 19 dBm, so P1dB,in = 0 dBm and the straight line at that input gives 20 dBm.

sections.h3: Two tones, IM3 and intercept points

blocks.text: Two-tone test: apply two equal sine waves at f1 and f2, each with input power Pin in dBm. A nonlinear amplifier produces mixing products. The dangerous ones are third-order intermodulation (IM3) products at 2f1 − f2 and 2f2 − f1. They sit close to the wanted tones, so a filter that passes f1 and f2 also passes them.

On a dB plot the wanted output per tone has slope 1: it rises 1 dB per dB of Pin. The IM3 output has slope 3: it rises 3 dB per dB. The two straight lines meet at the third-order intercept. The input intercept IIP3 is the Pin at that meeting in dBm. The output intercept is OIP3 = IIP3 + G, also in dBm.
OIM3 = 3(Pin + G) − 2 OIP3 = 3 Pin − 2 IIP3 + G
blocks.where: OIM3 is the third-order intermodulation output power per product in dBm; Pin is each tone's input power in dBm; G is gain in dB; IIP3 and OIP3 are the input and output intercept points in dBm.

blocks.text: The intercept is extrapolated: the amplifier compresses before the lines cross. IIP3 usually lies about 10 dB above P1dB,in. IM3 relative to the wanted carrier is OIM3 − (Pin + G), quoted in dBc. A more negative IM3 level in dBc means cleaner performance; −40 dBc is 10 dB cleaner than −30 dBc.

sections.h3: Dynamic range, blocking and spectral mask

blocks.text: Dynamic range is the span between the weakest and strongest usable signal. For a two-tone test, the lower end is the input-referred noise floor N in dBm. The upper end is where the IM3 output equals the noise floor referred to the output, N + G. Write the output IM3 as OIM3 = 3Pin − 2IIP3 + G and set it equal to N + G: 3Pin − 2IIP3 + G = N + G. The gain cancels, so 3Pin − 2IIP3 = N, which gives Pin = (2IIP3 + N)/3. The spurious-free dynamic range (SFDR) is Pin − N, in dB.

blocks.where: SFDR is spurious-free dynamic range in dB; IIP3 is input third-order intercept in dBm; N is the input-referred noise floor in dBm.

blocks.text: Blocking dynamic range uses the 1 dB compression point instead: BDR = P1dB,in − N. A strong off-channel signal compresses the amplifier and desensitizes the receiver. dBc is power relative to the carrier; dBm is absolute power. A spectral mask is the maximum allowed transmitter power versus frequency offset. Compression and IM3 spread energy outside the wanted channel and can break the mask.

Receiver selectivity and transmitter linearity are set together with the architecture. See 5.4 for where filtering and gain happen, and 5.5 for the transmit mask. Mixer-specific spurs belong to 5.7; power-amplifier linearization belongs to 5.8.

figure.caption: Output power against input power for a 20 dB amplifier. The measured curve bends below the straight line; at 0 dBm input the straight line gives 20 dBm but the measured output is 19 dBm.

spec.aria: Output power versus input power: the ideal straight line and a measured curve that bends near compression. At 0 dBm input the straight line gives 20 dBm and the measured curve gives 19 dBm.

examples.question: An amplifier has small-signal gain G = 20 dB, OIP3 = 30 dBm and a measured output 1 dB compression point P1dB,out = 19 dBm. Two input tones are each −10 dBm. Find IIP3, the ideal output per tone, the IM3 output level in dBm and dBc, and P1dB,in. State the straight-line output at P1dB,in.
steps: IIP3 = OIP3 − G = 30 dBm − 20 dB = 10 dBm.
Ideal output per tone = Pin + G = −10 dBm + 20 dB = 10 dBm.
IM3 relative to carrier = OIM3 − ideal output per tone = −30 dBm − 10 dBm = −40 dBc.
P1dB,in = P1dB,out + 1 dB − G = 19 dBm + 1 dB − 20 dB = 0 dBm.
Straight-line output at P1dB,in = P1dB,in + G = 0 dBm + 20 dB = 20 dBm; the measured output there is P1dB,out = 19 dBm, the 1 dB drop.
examples.answer: IIP3 = 10 dBm, ideal output per tone = 10 dBm, IM3 output = −30 dBm (−40 dBc), P1dB,in = 0 dBm, and the straight-line output at compression is 20 dBm while the measured output is 19 dBm.
examples.check:
G = 20.0
OIP3 = 30.0
P1dB_out = 19.0
Pin = -10.0
IIP3 = OIP3 - G
ideal_out = Pin + G
IM3_out = 3*(Pin + G) - 2*OIP3
IM3_dBc = IM3_out - ideal_out
P1dB_in = P1dB_out + 1.0 - G
straight_out = P1dB_out + 1.0
for value in [IIP3, ideal_out, IM3_out, IM3_dBc, P1dB_in, straight_out]:
    print(value)

traps: IIP3 is not a safe maximum input. It is an extrapolated intercept, usually about 10 dB above P1dB,in; driving to IIP3 is already deep compression.
Do not mix input and output intercepts. OIP3 = IIP3 + G. Using OIP3 where IIP3 belongs shifts the IM3 result by 2G.
The 3:1 slope applies to IM3 power versus each tone's input power in dB; the fundamental has 1:1 slope. Compare both against the same per-tone power.
P1dB,out is the measured output at compression, not the straight-line value. The straight-line output at P1dB,in is 1 dB above P1dB,out, and P1dB,in = P1dB,out + 1 dB − G. Watch that 1 dB.
dBc is relative to the carrier, dBm is absolute. SFDR needs an input-referred noise floor with IIP3, or an output noise floor with OIP3 used consistently.

quiz.a: P1dB,in is the input power in dBm at which the amplifier's actual output is 1 dB below the straight-line small-signal output.

quiz.q: Why does IM3 rise 3 dB per dB while the wanted fundamental rises 1 dB per dB?
quiz.a: The IM3 product is third order: its amplitude is proportional to the cube of the input amplitude. In dB, cubing multiplies the dB change by 3. The linear term is proportional to the input, so it rises 1 dB per dB.

quiz.q: An amplifier has G = 15 dB and IIP3 = 5 dBm. Two tones are each −20 dBm. Find the ideal output per tone and the IM3 output.
A receiver has input noise floor −100 dBm and IIP3 = −5 dBm. Find SFDR. If the noise floor rises by 6 dB, find the new SFDR and the change.
What is blocking in a receiver?
quiz.a: Blocking is a strong off-channel signal that drives an amplifier into compression and reduces gain for the weak wanted signal. The wanted signal is not at the blocker frequency, but the gain and noise change.

quiz.q: An amplifier has OIP3 = 35 dBm and G = 25 dB. Two tones are each −15 dBm. Find IIP3, the ideal output per tone, and the IM3 output.
Why is SFDR not simply P1dB,in − noise floor?
quiz.a: P1dB,in describes single-tone compression. SFDR describes the two-tone case where IM3 falls to the noise floor. IM3 grows three times faster than the fundamental, so the IM3 limit is reached before compression; SFDR is smaller and uses IIP3, not P1dB,in.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern radios use OFDM and other wideband signals with high peak-to-average power ratio, so average power runs well below P1dB. Digital predistortion and envelope tracking push power amplifiers closer to compression while holding the spectral mask. Cascaded IIP3 and memory effects decide system linearity in multi-stage transceivers. Search for “cascaded IIP3”, “digital predistortion”, “envelope tracking” and “memory polynomial PA model”.
